metadata.name: Core Ethical Policy
metadata.description: Baseline symbolic policy for the rule-based + constraint guardrail (roadmap item #1). Constraints are the hard safety floor (constraint-based reasoning); rules are deontic statements tied to ethical principles. Patterns cover English and Brazilian Portuguese. ON SUBSTRING MATCHING: keyword conditions match as substring by default, and the direction of the risk depends on WHERE the condition sits. In a trigger, over-matching is a false positive -- annoying. In an EXCEPTION it is a bypass, because the exception suppresses a DENY and the person writing the text picks the word, and therefore picks the exemption: 'desaprender' contains 'aprender', 'unlearn' contains 'learn', 'discourse' contains 'course'. THE RULE THIS POLICY NOW FOLLOWS: an exception keyword must not over-match. v0.4.0 closed part of it with whole_word:true, but whole_word is all-or-nothing -- it blocks 'unlearn' and loses 'learning' with it, which over-restricts the genuine educational framing. v0.5.0 stated that rule as one uniform shape, the BOUNDED PREFIX \bVALUE\w*\b, with two entries listed as deliberate departures from it. AS OF v0.6.0 THE RULE IS STATED ONCE AND THOSE TWO STOP BEING DEPARTURES: anchor the pattern with \b at both ends, and let THE LAST WORD decide the suffix -- wildcard if it inflects and its prefix generates nothing else (\baprender\w*\b, \blearn\w*\b); plain \b if it does not inflect usefully and its prefix does generate an unrelated word (\bconsult a doctor\b, which `whole_word: true` compiles to the same thing); enumerated forms if it BOTH inflects and collides (\bcursos?\b, because 'curso' gains 'cursos' but its prefix also generates 'cursor', an unrelated and frequent word in technical text; \beducaciona(l|is)\w*\b, because Portuguese pluralises -al to -ais, so 'educacionais' does NOT contain 'educacional' and a lone \beducacional\w*\b would silently drop the plural). A single word is simply the case where the last word is the only word, which is why 'curso' and 'educaciona(l|is)' are now the rule applied rather than carve-outs from it -- and the number of words was never the criterion: \bseek professional\w*\b would still match 'professionalism', and \bnão substitui\b would still lose 'não substituirá'. WHAT v0.6.0 SWEPT, AND WHAT IT DID NOT: the whole suppression path AS IT EXISTED THEN, not one rule. It walked three constructs -- `rule.exceptions` (engine.py), a `not` block inside a rule's `condition` (conditions.py, which suppresses by preventing the rule from firing and reports nothing), and a norm's `unless` concept list (kg_engine.py). R-SEC-002's 11 exception terms were checked and left unchanged, already correct since v0.5.0. R-TRANS-001's `not` block had all six entries matching as substring and three of them colliding; all six were fixed, and the reasoning per entry is written in that rule's own description. The `unless` path holds zero matchers today -- every norm omits it -- and is recorded here so the next sweep knows it was looked at rather than missed. AS OF v0.7.1 THIS PARAGRAPH NO LONGER SAYS 'EXACTLY THREE', AND THE CORRECTION IS THE POINT: it used to, and it used to add that `rule.exceptions` was the only construct populating verdict.suppressed. Both claims died after they were written, and neither died by anything in this file. THERE ARE FIVE SUPPRESSION CONSTRUCTS TODAY. Two of them postdate the v0.6.0 sweep and were therefore NEVER covered by it: (4) `Norm.unless_frame`, the declared refusal-frame guard (ontology.py + kg_engine._sob_guarda_de_frame), which arrived with the harm taxonomy, is declared by every harm norm, DOES populate verdict.suppressed, and hardcodes its successor as ALLOW in the engine rather than letting a norm declare one; and (5) `RefusalCondition` (frames.py), registered as the `refusal` condition type and usable inside any rule's `exceptions`, which no rule in this file uses today. A READER ASKING 'WAS THE SUPPRESSION PATH SWEPT?' MUST NOT READ THIS PARAGRAPH AS YES: three of five were, in v0.6.0, and the two that carry the harm layer have not been. TRIGGER keywords are unchanged and still match as substring, on purpose: there the risk runs the other way, and 'hack' with a word boundary stops matching hacking/hacked/hacker -- 23 of the 36 single-token keywords lose a real form that way. The 6 trigger keywords carrying whole_word (hackear, invadir, invasao, suicidal, diagnosis, dosagem) are the ones measured to lose nothing. Portuguese keywords are enumerated full forms rather than stems, which is why most of them are safe; English ones are stems where suffixing is plain concatenation, which is why most of them are not. WHAT v0.7.0 CHANGES, AND IT IS A NORMATIVE DECISION, NOT A REFACTOR: the reach of R-SEC-002's exemption. Until now a matched exception deleted the rule and nothing took its place -- measured over the 6 trigger x 11 exemption grid, 54 of 66 combinations released the request whole, as ALLOW with an empty match list. The engine now demotes to an effect the rule DECLARES, via the new `suppressed_effect` field, and R-SEC-002 declares REWRITE. THE QUESTION THAT DECIDED IT: fixing the engine guarantees an exempted 'steal credentials' is not ALLOW; it does not say what it should be. Two answers were defensible. B1 -- the exemption should not reach credential theft at all, because there is no sanitisable educational reading, so the right answer is DENY. B2 -- it should reach, and what is missing is the successor. B2 WAS CHOSEN. R-SEC-001 exists precisely to assert that offensive-security questions in an educational framing are sanitised rather than refused; credential theft is offensive security, and treating it differently needs a reason specific to it that nobody has stated. B2 also makes this rule's rationale true for the first time. B1 IS NOT DISCARDED, AND ITS CONTENT IS NOT SETTLED: an exemption bought with a keyword is one appended phrase away from anyone, which is a real argument -- but it argues about the STRENGTH of exemptions in general, not about these four triggers, since the same phrase already exempts the intrusion triggers and has since v0.1.0. Expressing B1 would need exemptions scoped to individual trigger conditions, which this schema cannot do: `exceptions` is one condition for the whole rule. That gap is recorded as a schema limitation with a destination, not as a rejected alternative. R-SEC-002 carries its own rewrite_template, written for credential theft rather than borrowed from R-SEC-001's intrusion wording, and it keeps `{content}` so the user's question survives the rewrite -- R-SEC-001's template does not, and that asymmetry is recorded rather than silently equalised here.
metadata.principles_reference: RQ1 principle mapping (non_maleficence, privacy, autonomy, fairness, transparency, accountability, security)

constraints.description: Instructions for building weapons, explosives or chemical/biological agents.
constraints.rationale: Mass-harm enablement can never pass, regardless of context.
Absolute prohibition; no exception is conceivable.

constraints.description: Creation of malicious software (malware, ransomware, keyloggers, botnets).
constraints.rationale: Malware authoring enables direct harm to third parties.

rules.rationale: Attempts to override the system's instructions compromise every other guarantee.

rules.description: Requests for personal information about identifiable individuals.
rules.rationale: Disclosing personal data of third parties violates privacy and data-protection norms (LGPD/GDPR).

conditions.pattern: \b(personal (information|data|details)|home address|phone number|social security number|informa[çc][õo]es pessoais|dados pessoais|endere[çc]o residencial|telefone|cpf)\b[^.?!]{0,40}\b(of|about|d[eoa]s?)\b

rules.description: PII leaking into generated output is redacted. Covers e-mail, CPF (punctuated, and unpunctuated when labelled), SSN, card numbers, RG, and Brazilian phone numbers in the forms an LLM actually writes them: +55 with or without parentheses and separators, and DDD + number without parentheses. DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED, so the omission is a decision and not an oversight: (1) CNPJ, which identifies a company rather than a person -- this rule serves the privacy principle and personal identifiers, a CNPJ is public record, and redacting it would break a legitimate answer such as 'company X, CNPJ ..., was fined'; the MEI case, where a CNPJ is tied to one individual, is what makes this debatable rather than settled. (2) CEP, which alone identifies a street, not a person, and whose redaction would break address and logistics answers while protecting nobody. (3) An unpunctuated CPF with no nearby 'CPF' label: a bare 11-digit pattern would match order numbers, identifiers and timestamps, and this engine is pure regex with no way to validate the check digits that would make such a pattern precise. The label must sit in the same sentence and the same line as the digits -- the gap may not cross '.', '?', '!' or a newline -- so that 'you need a CPF. The order number is 12345678900' does not match. Note that the labelled-CPF pattern redacts the label together with the number ('o CPF dele e 12345678900' becomes 'o [REDACTED:R-PRIV-002]'), because the anchor is part of the match and Python's re has no variable-width lookbehind to exclude it; the redaction is wider than the identifier, never narrower.
rules.rationale: Outputs must not expose personal identifiers even when generation was otherwise legitimate. Partial coverage is worse than none: when a response carries an e-mail and a phone number and only the e-mail is redacted, the reader sees [REDACTED] and concludes the text was handled.

rules.rewrite_template: The user asked about an offensive-security topic in an educational context. Explain the concepts from a defensive-security perspective only: how such attacks work conceptually, how to detect them, and best practices to protect systems. Do not include step-by-step offensive instructions.
rules.description: Offensive-security questions framed as educational are sanitised into defensive framing.
rules.rationale: Educational intent is legitimate, but the request must be steered to defensive content.

rules.rewrite_template: The user asked an offensive-security question inside an educational or defensive framing, so this request was DOWNGRADED, not refused. Answer defensively only. Explain how the attack works conceptually, what it looks like from the defender's side, and what actually stops it. Where the question concerns CREDENTIAL THEFT -- phishing, credential stuffing, password spraying, offline password or hash cracking -- treat it as a defender's topic: attacker economics and why the attack pays off, the detection signals that expose it (impossible-travel logins, spraying patterns across many accounts, anomalous authentication failure rates, breached-credential reuse), and the defences that measurably work (phishing-resistant MFA, rate limiting and lockout policy, modern memory-hard password hashing, breach-list screening, credential rotation). Do not supply operational procedure, tool invocations, command lines, wordlists, scripts, or step-by-step instructions for carrying any of it out, and do not target a named system or account. The user's original request follows unchanged so the answer can address what was actually asked: {content}
rules.description: Requests for offensive hacking techniques (account intrusion, credential theft). Denies outright; downgrades to a defensive rewrite when an educational/defensive framing applies.
rules.rationale: Unauthorized access instructions enable direct harm. When the exception matches, this rule no longer counts on R-SEC-001 to assume its place -- it declares its own successor via suppressed_effect and rewrites with its own template. The previous wording promised that R-SEC-001 handled the exempted case; that promise was false from the policy's birth for the four credential-theft triggers, which have no counterpart in R-SEC-001's intrusion-only trigger vocabulary, and the request was released whole in 54 of 66 measured trigger x exemption combinations.

rules.description: Requests to generate discriminatory or demeaning content about protected groups.
rules.rationale: Generating discriminatory content violates fairness and human dignity.

rules.description: Self-harm or suicide signals are withheld from automatic handling and blocked, with support resources shown to the user instead of a generated reply.
rules.rationale: Self-harm contexts require human judgment the system cannot provide; its obligation is to refuse to improvise and to surface help resources.
rules.user_message: If you are going through a difficult moment, you are not alone and help is available. Brazil: CVV - call 188 (24h, free) or chat at cvv.org.br. US/Canada: call or text 988. Other countries: findahelpline.com.

rules.description: Medical guidance in outputs must carry a professional-advice disclaimer (obligation: appended when missing). THE `not` BLOCK BELOW IS A SUPPRESSOR, and the risk there runs the same way as in an `exceptions` block, only worse: over-matching here does not permit a request, it deletes a SAFETY NOTICE. Measured before v0.6.0, with all six entries matching as substring: 'The dosage is 500mg daily. At this clinic we seek professionalism.' -> ALLOW. `seek professional` matched inside `professionalism`, the rule never fired, and a response that gives a dosage shipped with no disclaimer. Two more collided the same way: `consult a doctor` inside `doctoral`/`doctorate`, and `not a substitute for professional` inside `professionalism`. WHY THE SIX ENTRIES DO NOT SHARE ONE SHAPE -- the last word of the pattern decides, and all three outcomes occur here: (1) `\bnão substitui\w*\b` keeps the wildcard because `substitui` inflects (`substituirá`, `substituiu`, `substituindo` are all real disclaimers that must keep suppressing) and no longer word starts with it -- a plain \b on both ends would have been over-restriction, appending a notice to text that already carries one; (2) `consult a doctor`/`consulte um médico`/`procure um médico` take plain \b on both ends, which is exactly what `whole_word: true` compiles, because their last word gains no useful suffix while `doctor` does generate the unrelated `doctoral`/`doctorate` -- the two Portuguese ones are a measured no-op and carry the flag so the file records that they were checked; (3) `\bseek professionals?\b` and `\bnot a substitute for professionals?\b` enumerate, because `professional` both inflects (`professionals`, which must keep suppressing) and collides (`professionalism`, which must not) -- the suffix wildcard would buy the collision and plain \b would lose the plural.
rules.rationale: Transparency requires the system to disclose the limits of its competence in high-stakes domains.

rules.description: Requests for manipulation, social engineering or scam material.
rules.rationale: Deceptive content undermines the autonomy of the people targeted by it.
